claims.text: The baseline material is a W–Cu composite containing uncoated tungsten particles and consolidated by spark plasma sintering.
Physical vapor deposition can apply a uniform high-entropy-alloy nanolayer to tungsten particles before consolidation.
A Cr–Fe–Ti–Ta-based formulation is a suitable tailored refractory high-entropy alloy for the proposed interlayer.
Pre-coating tungsten particles will produce a nanometer-scale refractory high-entropy interlayer bridging the tungsten and copper phases after SPS.
The high-entropy interlayer will reduce thermal boundary resistance at the W–Cu interface.
The interlayer will improve electron transport across the W–Cu interface.
The refractory coating will maintain chemical stability during relevant processing and service.
Chemical stability of the coating will limit irradiation-induced defect nucleation.
Limiting irradiation-induced defect nucleation will preserve the composite's mechanical integrity.
The coated W–Cu composite will have significantly higher overall thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The coating will retain or improve mechanical durability relative to the uncoated composite.
The coating will retain or improve irradiation resistance relative to the uncoated composite.
SPS temperatures can be optimized to avoid detrimental interdiffusion and degradation of the nanolayer.
The predicted improvements should persist under high heat flux and moderate irradiation representative of fusion-reactor joints.
High heat flux and moderate irradiation are typical application conditions for fusion-reactor joints.
Retention of coating integrity during high-temperature SPS and prolonged irradiation has not been fully characterized.

The hypothesis is falsified if the coated material lacks a statistically significant thermal-conductivity improvement or exhibits degraded mechanical or irradiation resistance relative to the uncoated control.
